stem: During an outage of the central authentication service, a badge-controlled server room falls back to denying all entry until service is restored. Which secure design principle does this illustrate?
explanations: Failing securely means a component defaults to a secure, denying state when an error or outage occurs — exactly what the fallback behavior shows.
Least privilege limits the rights granted during normal operation; it says nothing about how a component behaves when it fails.
Separation of duties splits sensitive tasks between people to deter fraud; it does not describe failure behavior of a control.
Defense in depth layers multiple controls so one failure is not fatal; the scenario describes a single control's failure state, not layering.

stem: A vendor distributes firmware updates through public mirrors and must let devices confirm that each image is authentic and unmodified before installation. Which mechanism BEST meets this requirement?
options: A digital signature over each firmware image
A SHA-256 hash published beside each image
An HMAC computed with a shared device key
TLS encryption for every download session
explanations: A signature made with the vendor's private key gives both integrity and origin authenticity, and every device can verify it with an embedded public key without sharing any secret.
A hash alone proves integrity but not origin: an attacker who replaces the image on a mirror can just as easily replace the published hash beside it.
An HMAC requires the same secret in every device; extracting the key from any one device lets an attacker forge updates for all of them.
TLS protects data only in transit; a compromised mirror serves a tampered image over a perfectly valid TLS session.

stem: A military system must prevent users from reading documents classified above their clearance level. Which security model directly enforces this 'no read up' rule?
explanations: Bell-LaPadula is the confidentiality model whose simple security property forbids reading data above one's clearance — the 'no read up' rule.
Biba is the integrity mirror of Bell-LaPadula: it forbids reading down and writing up to protect data trustworthiness, not secrecy.
Clark-Wilson enforces integrity through well-formed transactions and separation of duties, not clearance-based reading rules.
Brewer-Nash, the Chinese Wall model, prevents conflicts of interest by restricting access based on a user's prior access history.

stem: A privileged installer checks a file's permissions, and an attacker swaps the file for a symbolic link in the instant between that check and the privileged write. Which vulnerability class is being exploited?
options: A buffer overflow in the installer
A time-of-check to time-of-use race condition
A privilege escalation via DLL injection
explanations: A buffer overflow corrupts memory through oversized input; nothing here involves the timing gap between validation and use.
Insecure direct object reference is a web authorization flaw where objects are reachable through guessable identifiers.
The attacker wins the race between the permission check and the privileged use of the file — the definition of a TOCTOU flaw.
DLL injection abuses library loading to run code inside another process; this scenario exploits filesystem timing instead.

stem: Researchers recover an encryption key from a smart card by passively measuring fluctuations in its power consumption during cryptographic operations. Which attack class does this represent?
explanations: Chosen-plaintext attacks analyze the mathematical relationship between selected inputs and their ciphertexts; they do not use physical emissions.
Power analysis recovers secrets from a device's physical leakage — consumption, timing, emanations — the defining trait of a side-channel attack.
Brute force exhaustively tries keys against ciphertext; no measurement of the device is involved.
Fault injection actively disturbs the device with voltage glitches or clock manipulation to cause exploitable errors; here the card is only passively observed.

stem: A data center wants to stop an unauthorized person from slipping through a secure entrance behind an employee's single badge swipe. Which physical control BEST addresses this?
options: Additional badge readers on interior doors
Security awareness posters at the door
explanations: Cameras are detective: they record the tailgating for later review but do not physically stop it.
Interior readers face the same weakness — the intruder simply follows an employee through each successive door.
Posters are an administrative nudge; a determined tailgater is not stopped by signage.
A mantrap's interlocking doors admit one authenticated person at a time, making tailgating physically impossible.

stem: A laptop fleet must release its disk encryption keys only when each machine boots with untampered firmware and boot loader. Which hardware capability provides this?
options: A Trusted Platform Module measuring the boot chain
A hardware security module in the data center
UEFI passwords protecting the firmware menu
explanations: A TPM records boot-component measurements in its registers and can seal the disk key so it is released only when those measurements match a trusted state.
An HSM safeguards keys for servers and applications centrally; it cannot attest to an individual laptop's boot integrity.
A self-encrypting drive protects data at rest but unlocks on its password regardless of whether firmware or boot loader were tampered with.
A UEFI password stops casual settings changes; it neither measures the boot chain nor gates key release on its integrity.
